label: Lakenvelder

about.text: The Lakenvelder is a traditional belted dairy cattle breed from the Netherlands and northwest Germany, with a belted coat. Wikipedia reports it from the Netherlands and Belgium today and possibly extinct in Germany.

links.name: Wikipedia: List of dairy cattle breeds

sources.text: Dairy breed and Netherlands and Belgium distribution with possible extinction in Germany, found in WebSearch result text from the Wikipedia cattle article (page not opened). The list article (opened by WebFetch) has a Lakenvelder row with Netherlands as its country, and gave no description of the breed. The 'traditional belted dairy breed of the Netherlands and northwest Germany' wording is the item's given line, not a source claim, and the 'Netherlands and Belgium' distribution is from the cattle article's search text.

origin.place: The Netherlands and northwest Germany; Wikipedia also reports Belgium today

sources.text: Origin in Netherlands and Germany, with the belted coat descending from Swiss and Austrian belted cattle (most likely account), from the Wikipedia article's text, found in WebSearch result text (page not opened). The Gurtenvieh link is listed as a theory, not as proven.
Described as a Dutch and German dairy breed in WebSearch result text from the Wikipedia article (page not opened).
Found in the Wikipedia cattle article's infobox, which cites DAD-IS, in WebSearch result text (DAD-IS itself was not opened).

gaps: The 'aka' 'Dutch Belted' from the item is not used: search results describe the Dutch Belted as a separate American dairy breed derived from Lakenvelder stock imported from 1838, so it is not the same animal. No names were confirmed. No DAD-IS population count was found. No milk, yield, composition or head figures found in the sources opened. The herd-book was started in 1918 and only five herds remained after 1930 regulations (Wikipedia, WebSearch result text) but that is history rather than formation, so it is not used as a formation date. Germany's status is uncertain (possibly extinct per Wikipedia). The Wikipedia 'Lakenvelder' page covers chickens, so only the cattle article was used.
